learning_outcomes.description: General learning objectives - Subdivide neural systems based on their functional roles and comprehend how these systems interact to produce goal-oriented behaviour.
General learning objectives - Identify structural components of the human brain and relate these to their functional importance, in both in health and disease.
Specific learning objectives - Identify the major subdivisions of the brain, its cellular components and/or support systems.
Specific learning objectives - Explain how sensory information is perceived and transmitted.
Specific learning objectives - Rationalise how motor output is generated and what brain structures are responsible for this expression of behaviour.
Specific learning objectives - Understand the importance of sensory feedback with regards to motor learning and the function of the cerebellum.
Specific learning objectives - Explain how the hypothalamus can sense physiological changes for maintenance of body homeostasis via neuronal and neuro-endocrine communication.
Specific learning objectives - Identify the hippocampus, its associated (limbic) structures, and understand the importance of these brain parts for learning and memory.
Specific learning objectives - Rationalise the importance of the brain's frontal lobe in higher cognitive tasks.
Specific learning objectives - Understand the brain areas and circuits that form the foundation for language and speech.

assessments.task_description:
The exam will comprise multiple-choice, short-answer and anatomy spotter questions on the theory and practical material covered in the first 12 lectures, 3 tutorials and 3 practical sessions.

The exam will be a closed book invigilated exam held on campus, undertaken via the Inspera Assessment platform. Students will be required to bring a laptop to the exam that meets the device requirements for Inspera. It is important that you check before the exam that your laptop meets the device requirements for using the Inspera Assessment platform. If you do not own a suitable laptop, you can borrow one from the Library. The Library website Get familiar with Inspera provides the latest information for students about using Inspera. Further information about the exam will be provided on Blackboard. 

Have your UQ student ID card available for all your exams.

This assessment task is to be completed in-person. The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools will not be permitted. Any attempted use of AI may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct.

learning_activities.topic:
LECTURE 1 & 2: Overview of the brain I & II

The first lecture will provide students with a general introduction to the course, including its structure, learning objectives, assessment requirements, and key themes in functional neuroanatomy (Lecture 1). We will then proceed to revise and/or familiarise students with the major subdivisions of the central nervous system, its support structures, and fundamental neuroanatomical terminology (Lecture 2). This lecture will include an overview of the cerebral lobes and their major functions, the ventricular system and cerebrospinal fluid circulation, the cranial nerves and their functional classifications, the organisation of the spinal cord, the peripheral nervous system, and the major arterial blood supply to the brain and spinal cord. This foundational knowledge will provide the anatomical framework required for understanding the functional organisation of the nervous system and the neurological disorders explored throughout the remainder of the course.


Learning outcomes: L01, L03

learning_activities.topic:
LECTURE 3 & 4: Cerebral Fluid Networks (Blood supply, cerebrospinal fluid & glymphatic system)

These lectures will introduce students to the fluid-based systems that maintain brain health and function. Lecture 3 will focus on the anatomical structures involved in brain protection and homeostasis, including the meninges, ventricular system, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and the arterial and venous blood supply of the brain. Students will examine how these interconnected systems provide nutrients and oxygen, remove waste products, and protect the central nervous system from injury and infection.

Lecture 4 will explore the glymphatic system, a recently described brain-wide clearance pathway that facilitates the movement of cerebrospinal fluid through neural tissues and promotes the removal of metabolic waste. Students will learn how the glymphatic system interacts with the cerebrovascular and ventricular systems, its role in maintaining neural health, and how its dysfunction has been linked to ageing and neurodegenerative diseases. Together, these lectures will provide an integrated understanding of the anatomical and physiological networks responsible for maintaining the brain's internal environment.


Learning outcomes: L02

PRACTICAL 1: Mandatory Gross Anatomy Facility (GAF) induction & overview of the brain

Mandatory Gross Anatomy Facility (GAF) induction

During this practical class, students will be introduced to the Gross Anatomy Facility (GAF), specifically in relation to OH&S regulations and the protocols that are to be followed when handling brain specimens. Students will become familiarised with the GAF space.

The accompanying practical class will provide an initial overview of the gross organisation of the nervous system, including the cerebral lobes, ventricular system, cranial nerves, spinal cord, peripheral nerves, and major blood supply to the brain and spinal cord.

Learning outcomes: L03

learning_activities.topic:
LECTURE 5 & 6: Reperfusion injury & Sensory systems I (spinal nerves and pathways)

Building on the concepts introduced in Lectures 3 and 4, which examined the brain's blood supply, cerebrospinal fluid circulation, and waste clearance systems, Lecture 5 will explore the consequences of disruption to these networks following cerebrovascular injury. Students will be introduced to the pathophysiology of ischaemia-reperfusion injury, including the cellular and molecular mechanisms that contribute to tissue damage following restoration of blood flow. The lecture will highlight the relevance of vascular anatomy and brain homeostasis to neurological disease and recovery.

Lecture 6 begins a mini-series on the major ascending sensory pathways that relay information from the body and external environment to the brain. Students will examine the organisation of spinal nerves, sensory receptors, and the principal ascending tracts of the spinal cord, including the dorsal column–medial lemniscus and anterolateral systems. The lecture will follow the journey of sensory information from the periphery through the spinal cord and brainstem to its final processing centres within the brain.

Learning outcomes: L02, L04

learning_activities.topic:
LECTURE 7 & 8: Sensory systems I & II

The final two lectures in this mini-series on sensory systems will focus on the specialised sensory pathways that allow us to perceive and interpret the external environment. Lecture 7 will examine sensory innervation of the head and face, with particular emphasis on the trigeminal system, before exploring the anatomy and functional organisation of the visual system, from the retina to the visual cortex. Lecture 8 will focus on the auditory and olfactory systems. Students will trace the pathways involved in hearing and smell from the peripheral sensory organs to their respective central processing centres and examine how these systems contribute to sensory perception.

Learning outcomes: L02, L04

learning_activities.topic:
LECTURE 9 & 10: Motor systems I & II (pyramidal & extrapyramidal tracts)

These lectures will examine the neural pathways responsible for voluntary movement and motor control. Lecture 9 will focus on the pyramidal system, including the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, and will trace the flow of motor commands from the cerebral cortex to skeletal muscles. Students will learn how these pathways are organised and how lesions at different levels of the neuraxis produce characteristic neurological deficits.

Lecture 10 will focus on the extrapyramidal motor pathways and their role in the regulation of posture, muscle tone, balance, and coordinated movement. Students will examine the major descending brainstem tracts and explore how these systems interact with the pyramidal pathways to produce smooth and effective motor function.

Learning outcomes: L02, L05

learning_activities.topic:
LECTURE 11 & 12: Motor system III & IV

These lectures will extend the discussion of motor control by examining two key brain regions that modulate and refine movement. Lecture 11 will focus on the anatomy and functional organisation of the cerebellum, with particular emphasis on its role in motor learning, coordination, balance, and the fine-tuning of voluntary movements. Students will explore how cerebellar circuits contribute to error correction and motor adaptation, and how cerebellar dysfunction manifests clinically.

Lecture 12 will focus on the basal ganglia and its role in the planning, initiation, and regulation of movement. Students will examine the major anatomical components and pathways of the basal ganglia and gain an understanding of how disruptions to these circuits contribute to common neurological disorders affecting movement.

Learning outcomes: L02, L05, L06

learning_activities.topic:
LECTURE 13 & 14: Hypothalamus & Appetite control

These lectures will examine the hypothalamus as a key integrative centre linking the nervous and endocrine systems. Lecture 13 will focus on the anatomy of the hypothalamus, its major nuclei, and its extensive connections with sensory, autonomic, endocrine, and limbic circuits. Lecture 14 will explore how these networks contribute to the regulation of appetite and energy balance. Students will examine the neural and hormonal mechanisms that influence feeding behaviour, satiety, and metabolism, and gain an understanding of how disruption of these systems contributes to disorders of appetite and body weight.

Learning outcomes: L07

learning_activities.topic:
LECTURE 15 & 16: Hippocampus & Thalamus

These lectures will examine two key integrative brain structures involved in learning, memory, and information processing. Lecture 15 will focus on the anatomy of the hippocampus, its extensive connectivity with other limbic structures, and its critical role in learning and memory. Particular emphasis will be placed on the neural circuits underlying spatial navigation and memory formation, as well as the consequences of hippocampal dysfunction.

Lecture 16 will focus on the anatomy and functional organisation of the thalamus. Students will examine the major thalamic nuclei and their connections with sensory, motor, and cortical regions of the brain, and will gain an appreciation of the thalamus as a key hub for integrating and relaying information throughout the central nervous system.

Learning outcomes: L07, L08

learning_activities.topic:
LECTURE 17 & 18: Sensory coding & cranial nerves

These lectures will explore how sensory information is represented and processed by the nervous system. Lecture 17 will introduce the principles of sensory coding, including receptive fields, stimulus intensity, modality, and the transmission of sensory information through neural circuits. Students will examine how the nervous system converts stimuli into meaningful neural signals and how these are interpreted by higher brain centres.

Lecture 18 will discuss in greater detail the origins, anatomy, and functions of those cranial nerves that were not covered in previous lectures. Particular emphasis will be placed on their sensory, motor, and autonomic components, as well as their functional roles in maintaining normal physiological function and behaviour.

Learning outcomes: L04, L05, L07

learning_activities.topic:
LECTURE 19 & 20: Language and speech & Clinical imaging

Lecture 19 will provide an overview of the neural systems underlying language comprehension and speech production. Students will examine the cortical and subcortical networks involved in language processing, including the functional specialisation of key brain regions and how damage to these areas can result in communication disorders. Particular emphasis will be placed on aphasia and other language impairments, and how patterns of dysfunction have contributed to our understanding of brain organisation.

Lecture 20 will focus on clinical imaging techniques used to investigate brain structure and function. Students will be introduced to imaging modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), functional MRI (fMRI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and positron emission tomography (PET), and will examine how these approaches are applied in both clinical practice and neuroscience research.

Learning outcomes: L02, L05, L08, L09

learning_activities.topic:
LECTURE 21 & 22: Prefrontal cortex & neurodegeneration

Lecture 21 will examine the anatomy and functional organisation of the prefrontal cortex, a brain region that is particularly well developed in humans. Students will explore how our understanding of the prefrontal cortex has evolved over time, from being considered a relatively “silent” region of the brain to one recognised as a critical regulator of executive function, decision-making, attention, behavioural flexibility, social cognition, and aspects of conscious awareness. The lecture will also examine the major connections of the prefrontal cortex with other cortical and subcortical structures and consider the consequences of prefrontal dysfunction.

Lecture 22 will provide an overview of neurodegenerative diseases and the mechanisms that drive progressive neuronal dysfunction and loss. Students will examine a range of disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, and motor neuron disease, and will be introduced to the cellular and molecular pathologies that characterise these conditions, such as protein aggregation, neuroinflammation, synaptic dysfunction, and neuronal degeneration. This lecture will also provide important background for the visit to the Integrated Pathology Learning Centre (IPLC), where students will have the opportunity to examine neuropathological specimens and relate anatomical changes to clinical disease.

Learning outcomes: L02, L08, L09

learning_activities.topic:
LECTURE 23 & 24: Associative striatum & psychiatric disorders

These final lectures in the integrative systems section will examine how distributed neural circuits contribute to higher-order cognitive function and how dysfunction within these networks can lead to psychiatric disease. Lecture 23 will focus on the associative striatum and its role in integrating information from multiple cortical regions to support executive function, decision-making, goal-directed behaviour, and cognitive flexibility. Students will examine the anatomical organisation of corticostriatal circuits and how information is processed within these networks.

Lecture 24 will build on these concepts by exploring how disruptions to cortical, limbic, and striatal circuits contribute to psychiatric disorders. Students will examine the neurobiological basis of conditions such as substance use disorders and schizophrenia and consider how advances in functional neuroanatomy continue to inform our understanding of complex psychiatric disorders.

Learning outcomes: L02, L08
